title: A Lock-Free SPSC Ring Buffer
summary: Build a fixed ring buffer, make it safe for one producer and one consumer with acquire and release, and pass a million ticks through it.
intro: A trading system is a chain of threads: one reads the exchange's feed, one runs the strategy, one sends orders. Between each pair sits a queue, and the system is only as fast as its queues. *Atomics and Memory Ordering* published data with a release store and an acquire load on one flag. This lesson builds the queue that pattern makes possible: a ring buffer for one producer and one consumer, with no lock and no allocation, the `SpscQueue<T, N>` that *Designing for Low Latency* reuses for its logger.

steps.title: A ring buffer in a fixed array
steps.body:
A feed handler thread hands every tick to a strategy thread. The blocking `TickQueue` from *Threads, Data Races, and Mutexes* works, but each push and pop locks a mutex, a waiting thread can sleep in the kernel, and its `std::queue` allocates as it grows. A **ring buffer**, like the one that carried ticks between two processes in *Processes Working Together: fork, Pipes, and Shared Memory*, keeps the items in a `std::array` of `N` slots, allocated once, and reuses the slots in a circle.

Two counters do all the work, and they only ever grow. `tail_` counts pushes and `head_` counts pops:

- The ring is empty when `head_ == tail_` and full when `tail_ - head_ == N`.
- A push writes slot `tail_ % N`, and a pop reads slot `head_ % N`.

Because the counters don't wrap at `N`, full and empty never look alike, and no slot is wasted. A `std::size_t` pushed a billion times a second would take 584 years to overflow, and unsigned subtraction stays right even then.

Make `N` a power of two and `% N` becomes the mask `& (N - 1)`:

```cpp
const std::size_t N = 4;
for (std::size_t tail = 0; tail < 6; ++tail) {
    std::cout << (tail & (N - 1)) << ' ';  // 0 1 2 3 0 1
}
```

With `N` a template constant, g++ already turns `% N` into that `and`. A size known only at run time costs a `div`, many times slower, where the mask stays one `and`. Here is g++ 10.2 at `-O2` for a `std::size_t i`, with the `ret` lines left out:

```text
; i % 1024, a constant
    mov  rax, rdi
    and  eax, 1023
; i % n, n known only at run time
    mov  rax, rdi
    xor  edx, edx
    div  rsi
    mov  rax, rdx
; i & (n - 1)
    lea  rax, [rsi-1]
    and  rax, rdi
```

A `static_assert`, from *Compile-Time C++: constexpr, static_assert, and Type Traits*, rejects any other `N` before the program runs.

example.title: Five prices into four slots
example.prompt: Push five prices into a four-slot ring, pop two, push two more so the ring wraps around, then drain it.
example.output:
push 101 ok
push 102 ok
push 103 ok
push 104 ok
push 105 full
pop 101
pop 102
push 106 ok
push 107 ok
drain 103 104 106 107
pop again empty
example.explanation: The first four pushes fill slots 0 to 3. Then `tail_ - head_` is 4, so the fifth push returns `false` and the caller decides what to do with 105. Two pops move `head_` to 2. Price 106 goes to slot `4 & 3`, which is 0 again, and 107 to slot 1, the two slots the pops freed. The drain reads slots 2, 3, 0, and 1, so the prices leave in the order they came. A pop on the empty ring returns `false` and leaves `out` alone.

practice.title: An order gateway queue
practice.prompt:
Finish `push` and `pop` for a four-slot ring of order ids waiting to go to the exchange.

1. In `push`, return `false` when the ring is full. Otherwise write `value` to slot `tail_ & (N - 1)`, add 1 to `tail_`, and return `true`.
2. In `pop`, return `false` when the ring is empty. Otherwise copy slot `head_ & (N - 1)` into `out`, add 1 to `head_`, and return `true`.
3. Leave `main` as it is: it reads `push <id>` and `pop` commands and prints what happened.

Input:

```text
push 7
push 8
pop
push 9
push 10
push 11
push 12
pop
pop
pop
pop
pop
```

Expected output:

```text
queued 7
queued 8
sent 7
queued 9
queued 10
queued 11
full, dropped 12
sent 8
sent 9
sent 10
sent 11
nothing to send
```

steps.title: Two threads: acquire and release
steps.body:
Now the feed thread pushes while the strategy thread pops, at the same time. Plain counters would be a data race, which is undefined behavior, so they become `std::atomic<std::size_t>`. That type is lock-free here: `std::atomic<std::size_t>::is_always_lock_free` is true on x86-64.

No lock is needed because each counter has a single writer. Only `push` moves `tail_` and only `pop` moves `head_`. The memory orders are the publish-then-flag pattern from *Atomics and Memory Ordering*, run both ways:

- `push` writes the slot, then stores `tail_` with `release`. A `pop` that loads that `tail_` with `acquire` is guaranteed to see the slot's contents.
- `pop` reads the slot, then stores `head_` with `release`. `push` loads `head_` with `acquire` before it reuses a slot, so it never overwrites one that's still being read.
- Each side loads its own counter `relaxed`, since no other thread writes it.

On x86 those acquire loads and release stores are plain `mov` instructions. This is `push` for `SpscQueue<long, 1024>` at `-O2`, its middle left out, then the same store with the default `seq_cst`:

```text
mov   rax, QWORD PTR [rdi+8200]    ; tail_.load(relaxed)
mov   rcx, QWORD PTR [rdi+8192]    ; head_.load(acquire)
...
mov   QWORD PTR [rdi+rdx*8], rsi   ; the slot
mov   QWORD PTR [rdi+8200], rax    ; tail_.store(release)

mov   QWORD PTR [rdi+rcx*8], rsi   ; the slot
xchg  rax, QWORD PTR [rdx]         ; tail_.store(seq_cst)
```

So `release` costs nothing here, and it still matters: it stops the compiler from moving the slot write below the store, and on ARM it compiles to a real store-release instruction. The rule that makes it all work is in the name, one producer thread and one consumer thread. Two producers would load the same `tail_` and write the same slot.

example.title: A million numbers between two threads
example.prompt: Pass the numbers 1 to 10^6 from a producer thread to a consumer thread through a 1024-slot queue, then check the count, the sum, and the order.
example.explanation: The `static_assert` would stop the build if the counters needed a lock. Each thread spins on its own core while the ring is full or empty instead of sleeping, a trade low-latency systems make on purpose. The sum of 1 to 10^6 is 500000500000, and every value arrived when expected, so none was lost, repeated, or reordered. `received` and `sum` can be plain variables because only the consumer touches them before `join`, which makes its writes visible to `main`. The first line, `// -O2`, makes the sandbox build it like `g++ -O2` in a terminal. Built that way, the million values took about 3 ms here, and about 65 ms through the blocking `TickQueue` design, rough times from the emulated sandbox.

practice.title: Trade prices with an end marker
practice.prompt:
Send trade prices from a producer thread to a consumer thread through an eight-slot queue, ending the stream with `-1`.

1. Finish `pop` like `push`: load `head_` relaxed and `tail_` acquire, return `false` when they're equal, copy the slot into `out`, then store `head + 1` with release.
2. Start a consumer thread that pops until it gets `-1`. For every other price it adds 1 to `count`, adds the price to `sum`, and keeps the highest in `high`.
3. Start a producer thread that pushes every price in `prices`, then `-1`, retrying each push while the queue is full.
4. Join both threads before the starter's print line.

Input:

```text
10050 10051 10049 10052 10050 10053 10048 10050 10051 10055 10054 10050
```

Expected output:

```text
trades 12, total 120613, high 10055
```
hints: `pop` is `push` turned around: `head` where `push` has `tail`, and `head_.store(head + 1, std::memory_order_release)` last.
In the consumer, `continue` when `pop` returns false and `break` on `-1`. Prices are positive, so `-1` can't be a real one.
`while (!q.push(p)) {}` retries until a slot is free.

steps.title: Ticks, cache lines, and cached counters
steps.body:
Each counter has one writer: the consumer writes `head_` and the producer writes `tail_`. When the two share a cache line, every write by one core pulls the line away from the other, the false sharing from *Memory Layout: Alignment, Padding, and Cache Lines*, which *Atomics and Memory Ordering* measured with real threads. So each side gets its own line with `alignas(128)`, the safe pad from those lessons: x86 lines are 64 bytes, but Intel CPUs fetch them in pairs, and Apple Silicon, which runs this sandbox under emulation, uses 128.

Padding alone didn't help, though. Built with `// -O2`, sending 10^6 `long` values took about 3 ms here with the counters together, and about 5 ms padded apart (rough and emulated). Both threads still read both counters on every call, so both lines bounced between the cores anyway. The fix is to read the other side's counter less often:

- The producer keeps `head_seen_`, the last `head_` it loaded, and loads `head_` again only when `head_seen_` says the ring is full.
- The consumer keeps `tail_seen_` and loads `tail_` again only when the ring looks empty.

Each copy sits on its owner's line, beside the counter that owner writes. Now each core mostly touches its own line, and the padding pays: about 2.2 ms. Caching without padding stayed near 3 ms, and some runs took ten times that. Emulated times are rough, so measure where you deploy.

As *Memory Layout: Alignment, Padding, and Cache Lines* noted, g++ 10.2 has no `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size`, so you write the number. The checked output is a size and a checksum: `sizeof` shows the padding, and a checksum over every tick, in order, shows none was lost.

example.title: A million ticks through padded lines
example.prompt: Pass 10^6 ticks through a padded `SpscQueue<Tick, 1024>` with cached counters, then print its size and a checksum of every timestamp, in order.
example.explanation: `sizeof` is 41216: one 128-byte line for the consumer's `head_` and `tail_seen_`, one for the producer's `tail_` and `head_seen_`, and 1024 slots of 40 bytes. `alignof` is 128 because of the `alignas` members, and C++17's aligned `new` keeps that true on the heap. The checksum multiplies by 31 and adds each `ts_ns`, so a lost, doubled, or swapped tick would change it, and a single-threaded loop over the same timestamps gives the same number. The `// -O2` first line builds it the way the times above were measured, and changes nothing that prints.

practice.title: Pad the queue and cache the tail
practice.prompt:
Give the queue a cache line per side and a cached tail, then checksum n ticks sent through it.

1. Put `alignas(128)` on `head_`, on `tail_`, and on `slots_`, so the consumer's data, the producer's data, and the slots each start a new 128-byte line.
2. Finish `pop` the way `push` uses `head_seen_`: compare `head` with `tail_seen_`, and load `tail_` with acquire only when they're equal.
3. In the consumer, fold each tick in with `checksum = checksum * 31 + ts_ns`, casting `ts_ns` to `uint64_t`.
4. The starter reads n, prints the size, sends the ticks, and prints the result.

Input:

```text
1000
```

Expected output:

```text
sizeof 10496
ticks 1000, checksum 7479348910764393760
```
hints: With the three `alignas(128)`, the size is 128 + 128 + 256 × 40 = 10496 bytes.
The checksum is a `uint64_t`, and unsigned arithmetic wraps without undefined behavior, so it can overflow safely.
In `pop`, when `head == tail_seen_`, set `tail_seen_ = tail_.load(std::memory_order_acquire)` and return `false` only if they're still equal.

recap:
- A ring buffer is a fixed `std::array` of `N` slots and two counters that only grow: empty is `head == tail`, full is `tail - head == N`.
- With `N` a power of two, the slot is `counter & (N - 1)`. For a template constant g++ turns `% N` into the same `and`, while a run-time `% n` is a `div`.
- One producer and one consumer need no lock, because each counter has a single writer.
- `push` writes the slot, then stores `tail_` with release. `pop` loads `tail_` with acquire, so it sees the slot. The same pair runs back through `head_`.
- On x86 acquire loads and release stores are plain `mov`s, and a `seq_cst` store is an `xchg`.
- Two threads prove the queue with totals and an order-sensitive checksum, printed after `join`.
- Padding the counters onto separate lines, 128 bytes to be safe, pays only once each side caches the other's counter and reloads it when the ring looks full or empty.

Next, **Beyond One Producer: MPMC Queues, ABA, and Seqlocks** lets many threads push and pop at once, and meets the bugs that come with it: ABA, freeing memory another thread reads, and torn reads.
